title: Dhruva's mantra
hookLine: a boy gets twelve syllables from a sage, and says them until God appears
carry: a mantra is the deity, in sound
tomorrow: why would anyone offer flowers to a drawing of triangles?

cards: A five-year-old prince tries to climb onto his father's lap, and his stepmother pulls him off. You're not my son, she says. If you want that seat, go and pray to the Lord.
The boy, Dhruva, takes her at her word. He walks out of the palace toward the forest. On the road, the sage Narada stops him.
Go home, Narada says, you're only a child. Dhruva won't. So Narada gives him something small to carry: a mantra.
Om namo bhagavate vasudevaya: I bow to the Lord Vasudeva. Twelve syllables. What can twelve syllables do?

teach.b: In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, Dhruva goes to a forest by the Yamuna and repeats the mantra month after month, eating less and less, until his whole attention lives inside it.
And Vishnu comes, and stands before the boy. Dhruva left home to win a seat on a lap; now he hardly wants it.
Vishnu gives him a place in the sky that never moves, and tradition links it to the pole star: Dhruva, the fixed one. Here's the teaching under the story.

In Hindu practice a mantra is received from a teacher, the way Dhruva received his from Narada, and then it's repeated. That repeating is japa: counted on a mala of beads, said aloud, whispered, or only thought.

teach.h: A MANTRA: THE DEITY IN SOUND.
teach.b: The Tantras say it boldly: a mantra is the deity's own form, in sound. A temple image is the god in stone; a mantra is the god in breath and voice.
The shortest are bija, seed syllables, like hrim, linked with the goddess. A seed doesn't look like a tree, but the tree is folded up inside.
And the texts treat a mantra as alive, its life handed down the line of teachers. Copied off a page, it's a seed kept in a drawer.
So a grandmother at six in the morning, beads sliding through her fingers, isn't stuck on a word.
Like Dhruva in the forest, she's keeping company with someone.

how: Practitioners repeat the mantra they received at initiation in japa, sometimes counting on a mala of beads, aloud, in a whisper or silently.

games.q: an app offers you 'your personal seed mantra' after a five-question quiz. in the tantric view you heard today, what's missing?
o: the teacher who hands it on, and with it the mantra's life.
nothing; a seed syllable works the same wherever you find it.
its meaning; once you know the translation, it starts to work.
games.why: the texts treat a mantra as alive through the line of teachers. copied off a page, or off a quiz, it's a seed kept in a drawer.

practice: Mantras like Dhruva's are given by a teacher, but many Hindus repeat a divine name freely: Rama, Krishna, Shiva, Durga. If there's a name you hold sacred, say it silently once on each out-breath, like one bead after another.
If you don't pray, let the soft sound of the breath be the thing you come back to.

wordCard.voice: What tantra actually is: here, a path built on mantra, the deity in sound, received from a teacher and kept alive in japa.

orig.note: Sanskrit bija, seed; the name for the shortest mantras, single seed syllables.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: a mantra is the deity, in sound. Dhruva found someone inside his. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 4.8–4.9 (Dhruva leaves home after his stepmother Suruchi turns him away; Narada gives him the twelve-syllable mantra om namo bhagavate vasudevaya; his japa in Madhuvana by the Yamuna; Vishnu appears and grants him the unmoving realm linked with the pole star)
Tantric teaching on mantra as the deity's form in sound (mantra-murti), e.g. Kularnava Tantra on mantra and on japa
